nameStory: This tiny plant earned its name from its floating lifestyle and the crystal-clear, gem-like appearance of its bright green branches when they catch the light underwater. The scientific name 'fluitans' literally means 'floating' in Latin, perfectly describing how these delicate mats drift freely on pond surfaces.
description: Floating crystalwort is a fascinating aquatic liverwort that looks nothing like the plants most people picture when they think of vegetation. Instead of leaves and stems, it forms bright green, branching ribbons that create dense, floating mats on the water's surface. These mats can spread quickly across ponds and quiet waters, looking like green lace floating just below or at the surface. Individual plants are quite small, but colonies can cover large areas of water.

idTips.label: Floating mats
idTips.description: Forms dense, bright green mats that float on or just below the water surface, feeling soft and spongy when gently touched

idTips.label: Branching pattern
idTips.description: Look for repeatedly forking, antler-like branches that feel delicate and break easily when handled

idTips.label: No true leaves
idTips.description: The green structures are flat, ribbon-like branches rather than separate leaves - run your fingers along them to feel the smooth, continuous surface

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Vibrant, almost luminous green that stands out clearly against dark pond water, especially when light filters through from above

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels soft and somewhat gelatinous when wet, with a delicate structure that compresses easily between your fingers

habitat: Look for floating crystalwort in quiet, still waters like ponds, slow-moving streams, and backwater areas throughout New England. It prefers nutrient-rich waters with good light exposure and is often found in the same habitats as duckweeds, though it may be crowded out by them. You'll typically find it in shallow areas where sunlight can penetrate to support its growth.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as water temperatures warm, with small green patches starting to appear on pond surfaces. This is when colonies begin expanding from overwintering fragments.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when dense, bright green mats are most visible and extensive. Colonies spread rapidly in warm, sunny conditions and are easiest to spot during this time.
seasonality.fall: Mats may begin to thin as temperatures cool, but colonies can persist well into autumn. Growth slows considerably as daylight hours decrease.
seasonality.winter: Most surface growth dies back, but fragments may survive in warmer microclimates or deeper water. Look for small remnants that will regrow in spring.

funFact: A single tiny branch fragment can grow into an entire colony covering large sections of a pond - aquarium hobbyists have learned that any small piece accidentally left in a tank can quickly take over the entire water surface!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with duckweeds, but floating crystalwort has branching, ribbon-like structures instead of duckweed's distinct oval leaves. Remember: crystalwort branches like tiny antlers, duckweeds look like miniature lily pads.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'wort' (an old English word for plant), crystalworts are liverworts, not flowering plants. They're actually more closely related to mosses than to typical garden plants, representing some of the earliest forms of plant life to colonize land millions of years ago.
compareHints: Floating crystalwort is unique among its New England relatives for its aquatic lifestyle - other crystalworts like Cavernous Crystalwort grow on moist soil rather than floating freely in water. While its relatives form small rosettes on land, floating crystalwort creates extensive surface mats and has much more elongated, branching structures adapted for life in water.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Cavernous crystalwort differs from floating crystalwort by growing on land rather than floating in water, and from other Riccia species by its distinctive surface pitting or caverns.

Violet Crystalwort differs from its cousin Floating Crystalwort by growing on soil rather than floating in water, and from Cavernous Crystalwort by its more delicate, thinner ribbons and distinctive violet tinge.
Unlike Floating Crystalwort which lives in water and has more delicate, thread-like segments, Lizard Crystalwort is terrestrial with broader, more substantial ribbons.
Unlike Floating Crystalwort which forms longer, more thread-like segments, Pond Crystalwort stays compact with shorter, broader ribbon segments.
Unlike Floating Crystalwort which lives in water, Frost's Crystalwort is strictly terrestrial and much smaller.
